resolved_defects.title: `x-datacompany-composition-point` was read by no code in either language
resolved_defects.as_recorded: EXTENSIONS.md section 6.4: 'It satisfies none of its apparent purpose. Nothing validates that the named $defs entry exists, that a domain schema attaches there, or that a schema without the annotation is non-extensible.' Recorded as a DECISION NEEDED -- give it an implementation, or retire it -- and as a liability: 'a declarative-only annotation in a vocabulary whose entire purpose is enforcement ... reads as a constraint and is not one'. merge_profile_extensions implemented the CONCEPT but was driven by its `extensions` argument and never consulted the member.
resolved_defects.taken: Implemented, in both engines with byte-identical message text, in two rules. (1) hash_profile._require_released_composition_point refuses, at DERIVATION, a value that is not a string beginning '#/$defs/' and one that does not RESOLVE to a $defs entry of the document the node belongs to. Resolution rather than a pattern match is the load-bearing half: '#/$defs/domian_extension' satisfies the meta-schema's composition_point regex exactly, survives every round trip and names nothing -- the typo hole a per-node pattern structurally cannot see. Resolved against the walk's current base $id, never against the entry schema, because a $ref into another released document reaches nodes whose pointers are relative to THAT document. (2) merge_profile_extensions refuses an extension offered to an envelope that declares no composition point; a schema without the annotation is NON-EXTENSIBLE. Presence is tested, not a null-valued read, so an explicit null reaches the malformed-value message rather than being reported as 'declares none'. The resolver's own error is deliberately NOT interpolated into either message -- see the residual finding below.
resolved_defects.rejected: Retiring the annotation, which was the other option on the table and would have deleted the only declarative statement an envelope makes about whether it invites extension at all. Also rejected: a positional check that an extension attaches AT the declared point. That is not derivable and would read stricter than it is -- the composition point names a $defs entry in SCHEMA space while included_pointers/arrays are RFC 6901 pointers in INSTANCE space, and every released composition point composes at the envelope root, so a declared point induces no constraint on which instance pointers an extension may name. The limit is stated in section 3.5, section 6.4 and both engines' docstrings rather than faked. Also rejected: re-implementing these rules as a JSON Schema validation of each node against the meta-schema, which section 9 item 13 forbids.
resolved_defects.hash_impact: NONE. x-datacompany-composition-point contributes no pointer, exclusion or ordering rule, so no manifest byte moves and no previously computed content_hash is affected. It changes WHETHER a manifest may be extended, not what one contains. Corpus blast radius, measured rather than argued: all six declaring envelopes resolve to a $defs entry that EXISTS, so no released schema became underivable; all 14 derivable schemas still derive, and the same four (locator-selector:1, page:1, release-ref:1, typed-refs:1) remain underivable for the pre-existing empty-included_pointers reason, unchanged from main. Every committed profile_extensions in the fixture corpus targets bitemporal-assertion:1, which declares a composition point, so no committed fixture route was closed.
resolved_defects.evidence: CORRECTION TO SECTION 6.4's OWN MEASUREMENT, which was wrong in both numbers and is fixed in the document: it said 'Three released envelopes declare it and three do not.' Actual, re-measured from the registry: SIX declare it in FOUR spellings -- '#/$defs/domain_extension' on bitemporal-assertion:1, immutable-version:1 and stable-identity:1; '#/$defs/problem_extension' on problem-details:1; '#/$defs/context_extension' on research-access-context:1; '#/$defs/manifest_extension' on run-manifest:1 -- and TWELVE do not. Section 3.5's 'all three released uses are the literal #/$defs/domain_extension' and the meta-schema's own $comment carried the same undercount and are corrected too. BEHAVIOUR CHANGE FOR CONSUMERS, checked per schema: the twelve are now non-extensible and each is INTENTIONALLY so, with the discriminator derived from the six declarers rather than assumed -- a composition point is a bare placeholder $defs entry ({"type": "object"} plus a $comment naming it). The detector finds that placeholder in 6 of 6 declarers (its positive control) and 0 of 12 non-declarers; no candidate is a near miss. Four of the twelve (locator-selector:1, page:1, release-ref:1, typed-refs:1) are $defs-only bundles with no root object that derive no manifest at all even on main, so 'non-extensible' was already their state; two (canonical-hash-profile:1, model-conformance-record:1) seal with additionalProperties:false; six (capability-status:1, evidence-location-candidate:1, evidence-location-version:1, identity-ref:1, pinned-version-ref:1, reference-verification-receipt:1) seal with unevaluatedProperties:false. Sealing is NOT the discriminator -- three of the six DECLARERS also seal with unevaluatedProperties:false -- which is why the verdicts rest on the placeholder entry. TESTS: fixtures/canonical-annotations/v1/refusals.json section 8.row7 carries four refusals (non-string, null, non-pointer, resolves-to-nothing) plus a repaired accepted control, each message read OUT of the engine and replayed byte for byte by both suites; the control previously named a $defs entry its own probe did not have, so under the new rule it was a refusal masquerading as a control. Plus tests/test_canonical_hash.py::test_an_envelope_declaring_no_composition_point_is_not_extensible, ::test_an_envelope_declaring_a_composition_point_is_still_extensible (the GREEN half, without which a refuse-everything gate passes), ::test_a_composition_point_that_resolves_to_nothing_is_refused_at_merge and ::test_a_composition_point_is_resolved_against_its_own_document, all mirrored in packages/typescript/test/manifests.test.ts. Mutations, each a real assertion failure: removing the whole merge gate is red ('DID NOT RAISE HashProfileError'); making it refuse EVERY envelope is red on the green half; removing only the merge-route resolvability re-check is red; resolving against the entry schema instead of the node's own document is red; replacing resolution with the meta-schema PATTERN is red on the typo case, which is the mutation that proves resolution is doing the work. tests/test_extension_vocabulary.py's DECLARATIVE_ONLY is now EMPTY -- every registered name in the vocabulary is read -- and its drift test still runs in both directions.
resolved_defects.residual_finding_not_introduced_here: PRE-EXISTING two-language message divergence in _require_released_schema_ref / requireReleasedSchemaRef, found while wiring the merge gate and NOT fixed (it is outside both decisions and its fix touches registry message text with repository-wide blast radius). Measured on the same forged manifest: Python emits `... declares schema_ref 'urn:datacompany:definitely-not-released:1', ... could never be built: unknown schema_ref 'urn:datacompany:definitely-not-released:1'` and TypeScript emits `... declares schema_ref "urn:datacompany:definitely-not-released:1", ... could never be built: unknown schema_ref urn:datacompany:definitely-not-released:1`. Two divergences in one message: `!r` versus JSON.stringify quoting, and the INTERPOLATED registry error, which renders with `!r` in Python and bare in the port. This is exactly the class section 9 item 13 forbids, and no fixture pins it -- refusals.json's replay dispatches only on derive_hash_profile and collect_cross_field_rules, so validate_hash_profile's messages are outside the record. The new composition-point messages deliberately do NOT interpolate the resolver's error, so this closure does not extend the class.

resolved_defects.title: What `equal` means across languages
resolved_defects.as_recorded: EXTENSIONS.md section 4.2: 'Under-specified: what "equal" means across languages. The engine uses Python ==. Verified consequences: true == 1 passes, 0 == false passes, 1 == 1.0 passes, "1" == 1 fails. A port using JavaScript === would reject the first three; a port using == would accept a different set again. No released rule can currently reach these cases ... so this document records the divergence rather than legislating it. A second implementation MUST use RFC 8785 canonical-byte equality ... Flagged for a spec decision.'
resolved_defects.taken: Both engines compare the RFC 8785 canonical bytes of the two values, for `equal` and `equal_when_both_present` alike. NOTHING NORMATIVE WAS INVENTED AND NOTHING WAS AVAILABLE TO INVENT: the same paragraph that recorded the divergence also prescribed the answer -- 'A second implementation MUST use RFC 8785 canonical-byte equality, which agrees with Python on every value the released schemas permit and is the same comparator unique_by and disjoint are being moved to (D1)' -- while the engine used ==. That is section 7.5's shape exactly: an unimplemented check is not an undecided question, and 'flagged for a spec decision' was the wrong label for a rule the document had already written down. It was also NOT hypothetical, which is the part the record understated: the TypeScript port had ALREADY moved to canonical bytes, so measured against both engines before the fix, {"left": true, "right": 1} and {"left": 0, "right": false} were reported HOLDING by Python and VIOLATED by the port -- the same released rule, the same instance, two answers. Python's bool IS an int, which no other language reproduces. SECOND, AND ADDED AFTER REFUTATION: an operand with no RFC 8785 canonical bytes is a RECORDED FAILURE naming the pointer, one per offending operand, left before right, and the equality verdict is not reached. The first version of this closure did not have that rule and was a REGRESSION for want of it -- routing `equal` through the canonicalizer turned a documented RETURN into a RAISE. allow_binary_float=True is not a blanket permit: it admits a finite non-integral float and does nothing for an int outside the exact IEEE-754 double range, for NaN/+-inf, or for a lone surrogate, and all four arrive through stdlib json.loads on its DEFAULT settings. Measured, {"evidence_location_id": 9007199254740993, "entity_id": 9007199254740993} against evidence-location-version:1 returned 16 failures before the change and raised UnstableFloatError after; validate_instance deliberately concatenates the schema layer and the cross-field layer rather than short-circuiting, so malformed input -- the case it exists to describe -- was exactly the case that began throwing. The rule was DERIVED, not chosen: section 4.1 already decided the identical question the identical way, an interval bound that is not a released instant being 'a recorded failure, never a comparison'. The message interpolates POINTERS only and names no value, because the two engines' own exception text for the same input already differs (nan here, NaN in the port) and rendering the value would import the unclosed repr-versus-canonical divergence recorded as EXT-4.5-residual.
resolved_defects.rejected: Legislating JavaScript ===, which is reference identity for objects and would make {"a":1,"b":2} unequal to {"b":2,"a":1} -- one JSON value written twice, and exactly the Python-only-representation error D1 removed from unique_by and disjoint. Also rejected: leaving section 4.2 as a recorded divergence on the ground that 'no released rule can currently reach these cases'. That is a fact about today's schema constraints, not a property of the engine, and check_cross_field_rules is a public schema-independent entry point -- the same reasoning D2c was closed against. Also rejected, and this one was proposed by the reviewer: reporting an uncomparable operand as UNEQUAL. Having no canonical bytes is a different fact from differing, and collapsing the two would let a value the contract cannot represent be reported as a decided inequality; section 4.1's precedent is explicit that such a case is a recorded failure and never a comparison.
resolved_defects.hash_impact: NONE, and measured rather than argued, three ways. (1) All 18 released schemas were derived and validated before and after; the two manifest sets diff EMPTY, under a positive control that plants an x-datacompany-hash-excluded on model-conformance-record.v1 /package_id and produces a non-empty diff. This is a validation rule and not a derivation rule, so DERIVATION_PROFILE_VERSION did not bump for this change. (2) The three released equal/equal_when_both_present sites produce 40 present operand pairs over every committed JSON document and the two comparators agree on all 40, while the control pairs true/1 and 0/false disagree -- a zero measurement without a positive control is an absent one. (3) Re-measured after the regression fix, far wider than the original claim: every JSON object to depth 6 across fixtures/, examples/, schemas/, model-conformance/ and compatibility/ crossed with all 18 released schemas = 39006 (instance, schema) pairs, ZERO raises on either side, and exactly ONE differing pair -- which is the new EXT-4.5 vector this branch itself adds. Excluding that one new fixture file: 36936 pairs, ZERO differences, positive control 1 -> 3 failures.
resolved_defects.evidence: fixtures/canonical-cross-field/v1/operator-vectors.json, 23 vectors replayed against the EXACT failure list, element by element and in order, by tests/test_cross_field_operator_vectors.py and packages/typescript/test/crossFieldOperatorVectors.test.ts. Ten are section 4.2 (7 expecting a failure, 3 expecting none) and they discriminate the candidate readings SEPARATELY: true/1 and 0/false must FAIL (rules out Python ==), "1"/1 must FAIL (rules out JavaScript ==), 1/1.0 must PASS (rules out comparing source text), {"a":1,"b":2}/{"b":2,"a":1} must PASS (rules out JavaScript ===), a lone surrogate must be a NAMED FAILURE (rules out the raise). The per-section failing/passing split is an EQUALITY in both suites, not a floor: without the passing vectors an engine that reported every pair as violating would satisfy every failing vector in the file. ONE vector carries a declared per-engine expectation and the COUNT of such declarations is pinned as an equality in both languages, so a second divergence cannot be admitted by quietly adding a key; that one is not an engine defect and no engine change removes it, because JSON.parse collapses an integer literal outside the exact double range before the port's engine runs while json.loads yields the exact int -- so {"left":9007199254740993,"right":9007199254740992}, two DIFFERENT JSON integers, is undecidable in Python and HOLDS in the port. NaN and +-Infinity are the mirror image, unwritable in strict JSON, and are covered by an in-code test in each suite. A separate test drives the divergent pair through a RELEASED rule rather than the probe, so the closure cannot be test-only. Replayed against origin/main's engines the final record is red 20/32 in Python and 15/31 in the port. tests/mutation/cross_field_operators.py carries 35 mutations, ALL RED, including reject-everything and accept-everything in both languages and three that restore the raise.

resolved_defects.title: unique_by reports / disjoint silently skips a member missing its key
resolved_defects.status: CLOSED 2026-08-04. The rendering divergence recorded as EXT-4.5-residual is a DIFFERENT defect and is not closed.
resolved_defects.as_recorded: EXTENSIONS.md section 4.5: 'A member missing its key is a reported failure in unique_by (step 2) and a silent skip in disjoint (steps 2 and 3). Re-verified against 377c1b6: a right member of {"nope": 1} under right_key: "/p" still produces no failure. ... Both behaviours are defensible in isolation; they cannot both be right. Needs a spec decision -- this document does not pick one.'
resolved_defects.taken: disjoint reports it, on BOTH sides, aligned onto unique_by, in both engines and through one shared message helper so the two cannot diverge again: '<name>: <side>/<i> does not carry the disjointness key <key>'. Failure ORDER is now contract text -- the left walk, then the right, each in index order -- because two engines reporting the same two failures in different orders diverge on the joined message. THE SIDE WAS NOT PICKED HERE; the repository had already picked it, in released code, for the identical question: the hash view refuses a set-like array whose member lacks its order key (MissingOrderKeyError) because 'every member of a set-like array must carry its whole released order key, and an absent key is not the same fact as a shared one'. Skipping in silence is the fail-open direction and 'the two sets are disjoint' being true by vacuity one member at a time is the class this repository exists to eliminate. A member whose key is missing contributes no value either, so the left set is still built from the members that do carry the key; the change is that the ones that do not are now named. SCOPE CORRECTION: an earlier version of this entry said the two released canonical-hash-profile:1 disjoint rules were untouched. That is true of their LEFT side only. Both declare right_key: "/pointer", so their right side can now report a failure they did not report before -- {"included_pointers": ["/a"], "excluded_pointers": [{"nope": 1}]} produces two 'does not carry the disjointness key /pointer' lines that 377c1b6 does not produce. Bounded rather than absent: pointer is required under additionalProperties: false, so a manifest in that state already fails the schema layer -- but check_cross_field_rules is a public, schema-independent entry point, which is the same reason D2c was closed. EXTENSIONS.md section 4.5 now says left side only and the shape carries its own vector. EXTENDED 2026-08-04, same commit: unique_by and disjoint also called the canonicalizer on a member key UNGUARDED, so a member key with no RFC 8785 representation made check_cross_field_rules raise where it is documented to return failures. That is EXT-4.2's defect in the operators that had it for the same reason, and both are fixed together rather than disjoint alone -- fixing one would have re-opened the very section 4.4 / section 4.5 asymmetry this entry closes. Same message as EXT-4.2's with the proposition named ('so the uniqueness cannot be decided' / 'so the disjointness cannot be decided'), same left-before-right ordering, both engines.
resolved_defects.rejected: Aligning unique_by onto disjoint -- i.e. making unique_by skip too. It is the fail-open half of the choice, it contradicts the hash view's released decision on the same question, and it would change a released failure message. Mutation M10 makes exactly that edit and is RED. Also rejected: reporting a member as missing its key on a side that declares NO key. A member compared whole has no key to be missing, and reporting one would reject every committed hash manifest -- the two released canonical-hash-profile rules are asymmetric with a bare-string left side. Mutation M9 makes that edit and is RED against a dedicated control vector. Also rejected: recording the unique_by/disjoint raise as pre-existing residue and closing section 4.5 without it, which is what the first version of this branch did. Leaving a known raise in a released validation path immediately after fixing its twin is half a fix, and the asymmetry argument that justifies fixing disjoint at all is the argument for fixing both.
resolved_defects.hash_impact: NONE, and measured. All 18 released manifests are byte-identical before and after, under the same planted-exclusion positive control as EXT-4.2; this is a validation rule, so DERIVATION_PROFILE_VERSION did not bump for this change. Blast radius over the corpus is zero WITH a control, in both halves. Missing-key half: every committed JSON document crossed with all three released disjoint rules gives 23 array pairs actually evaluated and 466 members inspected, none of which lacks its key, and the control plants {"nope": 1} into a real corpus instance and is seen 23 of 23. Uncomparable-key half, measured BEFORE extending so that no committed fixture's asserted text could move: 10835 evaluations of the five released unique_by/disjoint sites over every JSON object in the corpus, ZERO of which raise today, under a positive control confirming that a lone surrogate in a member key DOES raise. Every failure the extension adds is therefore on an input that previously crashed, never on one that previously reported. Whole-corpus recheck after both halves: 39006 (instance, schema) pairs, zero raises, exactly one differing pair, and that pair is this branch's own new vector.
resolved_defects.residual_divergence: SECTION 4.5 IS CLOSED; disjoint's OVERLAP message is still not byte-identical across the engines and this entry must not be read as claiming it is. Python interpolates the offending value with repr and the port with RFC 8785 canonical text: 'a' versus "a", True versus true, None versus null (unique_by on a duplicate null), 'notalist' versus "notalist" (the non-array-target message). Reachable on run-manifest:1, the one released disjoint rule that can fire, whose members are UUID STRINGS. What IS byte-identical by construction is every message this closure ADDED -- the missing-member-key and uncomparable-operand messages interpolate pointers only. Carried as EXT-4.5-residual for the open register; see the note beside it about where that entry can go.
resolved_defects.evidence: fixtures/canonical-cross-field/v1/operator-vectors.json, 13 section 4.5 vectors (11 expecting a failure, 2 expecting none) replayed against the EXACT failure list by both engines: a missing key on the left, on the right, on both (which pins the order), a missing key that used to HIDE a real overlap, the overlap itself, a side with no declared key that must report nothing, the RELEASED asymmetric shape with right_key and no left_key, unique_by's unchanged released message, an uncomparable member key in unique_by and on each side of disjoint, and a mixed left-missing/right-uncomparable case that pins the two kinds interleaving in one walk. The two expecting no failure are the false-positive controls; without them an engine that reported every member as bad would satisfy the whole set. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO A CLAIM THIS ENTRY PREVIOUSLY MADE: unique_by's message is NOT pinned by any committed fixture through expected_error_contains. Measured: 80 fixture files use expected_error_contains and ZERO of them contain 'does not carry the uniqueness key'. It was pinned by nothing at all until this branch's vector existed. The earlier wording cited that non-existent pin as grounds for rejecting an alternative, which is the false-provenance class this repository keeps finding; the text is byte-preserved regardless, and the vector is now the pin. tests/mutation/cross_field_operators.py carries 35 mutations, ALL RED, including restoring the silent skip on each side, flipping the order, reporting every member as missing, removing each uncomparable guard so the engine raises again, and rewording the shared message by one article, in both languages.
